# Grigorii Moskalev — Legal counsel and legal engineer

> Grigorii Moskalev is a legal counsel who builds AI tools for legal teams. 11 years practicing law, 3 years writing Python. Author of PII Shield (open-source MCP server that anonymizes documents before LLM analysis), memoforge (Cowork plugin that drafts footnoted legal memos), Brand monitor (trademark-infringement scanner), and Plain (lightweight Markdown reader and editor for Windows and macOS). Based in Limassol, Cyprus.

This file is the long-form Markdown export of gmoskalev.com for LLM ingestion. The slim index is at [llms.txt](https://gmoskalev.com/llms.txt).

# About

11 years practicing law, 3 years writing Python, and a growing overlap between the two. I run the legal function at a consumer tech product used by hundreds of millions, across IP, privacy, corporate, and app-store disputes. Before that, KPMG and senior in-house roles at international tech companies across Cyprus, the EU, and beyond.

Legal engineering is what I genuinely love. I've built RAG pipelines over our internal corpus, contract analytics, MCP servers that keep client data off the API. I work with prompt engineering and fine-tuning, and I deploy local models when client data shouldn't reach a hosted one in the first place.

I've also shipped legal-tech projects as a product owner, taking ideas from zero to launch and owning the spec, the flows, and the API.

# Projects

## PII Shield

- **Tagline:** Anonymize documents before Claude sees them. Restore real data after analysis.
- **Status:** Live. Current version and builds: https://github.com/gregmos/PII-Shield/releases/latest
- **Repo:** https://github.com/gregmos/PII-Shield
- **License:** MIT
- **Stack:** Node.js, MCP, GLiNER, ONNX, DOCX

MCP server for Claude Desktop. Reads documents locally, swaps every name, ID, and number for placeholders (`<PERSON_1>`, `<ORG_1>`, etc.), and sends only the anonymized text to Claude. After analysis, the real values are stitched back into the final document — all on your machine. PII never enters the API.

## memoforge

- **Tagline:** From one legal question to a finished .docx memo.
- **Status:** Live. Current version and builds: https://github.com/gregmos/memoforge/releases/latest
- **Repo:** https://github.com/gregmos/memoforge
- **License:** MIT
- **Stack:** Cowork plugin, 15 agents, IRAC, MCP citations, python-docx

Cowork plugin that mirrors a small legal team. A triage analyst clarifies missing facts; three researchers pull statutes, case law, and regulator guidance in parallel; a currency check confirms the law is still good; a writer drafts in IRAC; five reviewers stress-test the draft on logic, citations, style, clarity, and contrary authority; a mediator consolidates the findings; and the writer revises up to three rounds before a client-readiness polish and `.docx` export. Two modes — Brief (2–3 pages, statutory research, 3 reviewers, 1 revision) and Full (5–8 pages, statutes + case law + doctrine, all 5 reviewers, up to 3 revisions, polish). Bundles two MCP servers — Legal Data Hunter for multi-jurisdictional law and CourtListener for US case law — with a WebFetch fallback to official portals. Every memo ships with the full source pack, per-reviewer findings, and an honest verdict (`approved`, `forced_exit_on_v3`, or `manual_review_required`). Optional Style Studio turns a folder of example memos into a saved house-style profile. Runs locally — no shared backend, no telemetry.

## Plain

- **Tagline:** Double-click a .md file and you are reading.
- **Status:** New. Current version and builds: https://github.com/gregmos/plain/releases/latest
- **Page:** https://gmoskalev.com/plain
- **Repo:** https://github.com/gregmos/plain
- **License:** MIT
- **Downloads:** Windows zip (single plain.exe, code-signed) and macOS 13+ universal dmg (Developer ID signed and notarised) from the latest GitHub release — https://github.com/gregmos/plain/releases/latest
- **Stack:** Tauri 2, Rust, React 19, TypeScript, CodeMirror 6, unified (remark/rehype), Shiki, KaTeX, Mermaid

A lightweight Markdown reader and editor for Windows 11 and macOS. Three views of one document: `read` renders it, `edit` shows the source with syntax highlighting, `rich` shows the source with the markup hidden (Typora-style); `split` puts edit and read side by side. Switch with `Ctrl+/` or the mode bar; caret and scroll position survive the switch.

Markdown support: CommonMark + GFM (tables, task lists, footnotes, strikethrough), callouts (`> [!note]`, tip, warning, important, caution), KaTeX math, Mermaid diagrams, Shiki-highlighted code, `==highlights==`, `[[wikilinks]]`, YAML front matter, images from the folder (paste or drop saves into `assets/`), `#tags`, sanitised inline HTML. Every construct has a command: `edit → insert`, the command palette, `Ctrl+Alt` shortcuts, and an optional one-row formatting toolbar.

A folder is the library: file tree (create, rename, delete to Recycle Bin/Trash), quick open `Ctrl+K`, full-text search `Ctrl+Shift+F` (Rust, parallel, case and regex toggles), library screen `Ctrl+Alt+L` with dates, word counts and `#tag` filter, tags and backlinks in the sidebar, version history (a snapshot of every save kept 30 days, restore and compare). No index, no cache, no service files in the user's folders.

Careful saving: bytes the user did not touch do not change (list markers, indentation, trailing spaces, BOM, final newline); CRLF/LF preserved (mixed files normalised to the dominant style with a status-bar message); UTF-8, UTF-8 BOM and UTF-16 written back as read; legacy cp1251 converted to UTF-8 only after confirmation; atomic writes via temp file + replace with a hash check against the file on disk; external changes reloaded quietly when there are no local edits, otherwise a banner with reload / save my copy as / compare; recovery drafts within 2 seconds of every change; `Ctrl+S` on an untouched buffer writes nothing; optional autosave (off by default).

Interface: IBM Plex Mono everywhere, one accent colour, no icons, light and dark themes following the system. Shortcuts bind to physical keys (work in Cyrillic layouts); on macOS ⌘ replaces Ctrl with a few remaps. Settings (`Ctrl+,`, one small `settings.json`): theme, font size, content width, line numbers, toolbar, indent unit, code wrap, autosave, new-file EOL, library extensions, tags.

Data lives in `%APPDATA%\Plain` (Windows) or `~/Library/Application Support/Plain` (macOS): `settings.json`, `drafts/`, `state.json`, `history/`. A `data` folder next to `plain.exe` enables portable mode on Windows.

Limits by design: no plugins, sync, cloud, AI, telemetry, auto-update, database or index; no localisation or custom keymaps yet; renaming a file does not update links. Memory is WebView2/WKWebView-sized (around 180 MB private with a file open). Personal project built in the evenings; the macOS build comes from CI and has had less time on real hardware.

## Brand monitor

- **Tagline:** Find the apps stealing your name and the sites cracking your build — every week, on autopilot.
- **Status:** Live
- **Repo:** https://github.com/gregmos/Brand-monitor
- **Stack:** SKILL.md, iTunes API, Vision, WHOIS, Excel

Skill that scans the App Store and the open web for knockoffs and cracked APKs of your app. iTunes Search across countries plus fuzzy-matching narrows ~1,000 listings to ~50 real candidates; icon vision and WHOIS-backed evidence packages confirm the rest. An LLM layer scores risk, recommends action, and ships a prioritized Excel report. The whole thing is a single SKILL.md — drop it into Claude or OpenClaw, tell it your trademark and target countries, and it runs itself. Hours of manual work → ~20 minutes of review.

# Writing

Notes on legal-AI work — originally posted on LinkedIn. Live index: https://gmoskalev.com/writing

## Plain: a free Markdown reader and editor, because $15 was too expensive (7 Sep 2026)

I have a $200 Claude subscription. Obviously, a $15 .md reading/editing app was too expensive to buy. Almost everything I get out of LLMs these days is markdown; I wanted a comfortable way to read and edit it. I could have bought Typora. Instead, I built Plain, a free, open-source Markdown reader and editor for Windows and macOS, and honestly I like it better than the $15 option. Inside: three views of the same file (reading, syntax-highlighted source, rich editing with the Markdown syntax hidden) plus a Word-style formatting toolbar and split view; tables, checklists, footnotes, callouts, KaTeX formulas, Mermaid diagrams, and images pasted from the clipboard; any folder becomes the library with a file tree, quick file search, full-text search, tags and backlinks; careful saving (anything you haven't edited stays untouched byte for byte, atomic saves, crash recovery drafts, 30-day version history, a warning if another app changes the file); fully local with no server, account or database; dark/light mode and export to HTML and PDF. MIT-licensed; source and installers (exe and dmg) on GitHub. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_i-have-a-200-claude-subscription-obviously-activity-7502624765489094656-ZIAD)

## Legal engineer: a salesman, a builder, or both? (3 Sep 2026)

Harvey's Legal Engineer program describes someone who has practiced law, knows LLM basics, thinks in workflows, explains things in plain terms and sees the pain points of a legal department: a connector between the solution and the customer. Fair enough; the biggest problem of legal AI is not hallucinations, it is adoption. In-house legal engineer job posts shift the focus to knowing the tools on the market and matching tool to process. Neither asks a legal engineer to build, although "engineer" is right there in the title. My take: a legal engineer is basically a product manager for legal work. He builds hypotheses, tests them, puts together an MVP, breaks it, rebuilds it, looks at the data, designs the workflow and the user experience. Building is not a prerequisite, it is the fastest way to test a hypothesis in 2 days instead of a month. First of all someone with product and commercial thinking (KPIs, pains, how to close them), good with data, able to measure the actual effect. Salesman or builder? Both are just tools. The job is to find the right problem and prove you fixed it. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_legal-engineer-is-a-salesman-a-builder-or-activity-7501214065789337600-Hmc5)

## PII Shield now runs as a CLI (17 Jun 2026)

Anonymize any document locally before it reaches an LLM, then restore the real data on your machine. 35 entity types across 17 jurisdictions, on-device, open source. Build it into your workflow; open a PR or an issue and say what it misses. Install: npm install -g pii-shield. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_pii-shield-now-runs-as-a-cli-anonymize-activity-7472925841824350209-kriG)

## Shared matter context: the next battleground in legal tech? (12 Jun 2026)

Most legal AI tools are built for one of two situations: a lawyer working alone, or a team inside one company. But a big chunk of legal work happens between two organizations, in-house and outside counsel, and that work still runs on email and attachments. In-house knows why the question came up and how much risk the business can actually live with; the firm knows how the market usually handles it. So each side's AI only sees its own half of the picture. Harvey and Legora are moving in this direction, but privilege, confidentiality, conflicts and hourly billing look much harder to solve than the tech itself. Will shared matter context become the next battleground in legal tech, or does the trust problem kill the idea? (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_most-legal-ai-tools-are-built-for-one-of-activity-7471147635932815360-UWR0)

## Mourning the junior lawyer misses the actual problem (9 Jun 2026)

Part of my feed is mourning the junior lawyer, killed off by AI: no entry-level work, no way to learn, no path to senior. Firms have always trained juniors the way guilds trained apprentices: watch a senior, copy them, slowly pick it up over years. AI now does a lot of that entry-level work, but that work was never the point; it was how juniors absorbed judgment and a feel for how the firm thinks. Meanwhile a firm produces dozens of documents, hundreds of calls and constant research every day, and almost none of that expertise is saved or reused. It was never fixed because writing down how you think doesn't bring in fees. That's what changed: AI can do the costly part for almost nothing (summarize the call, pull the reasoning out of a thread, turn a finished matter into something a junior can study), and it all has to come together into one layer of what the firm knows today, with training that corrects itself as new work comes in. That's the new apprenticeship: what took years could take months. Not all of it transfers (when to push a client, how to read a room), but juniors clear the teachable part far faster. Instead of one more post mourning the junior lawyer, do something with the data already sitting inside your own firm. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_part-of-my-feed-is-mourning-the-junior-lawyer-activity-7470007107212455939-5CbE)

## memoforge: free, cited, verifiable memoranda in your Claude Cowork (2 Jun 2026)

Ask a general-purpose LLM for a legal memo and the output is fluent but generic; you can't verify it fast enough to trust it, and on a contested question it quietly picks a side. memoforge is an open-source plugin for Claude Cowork and Claude Code that turns one legal question into a finished, footnoted .docx memorandum. It runs a multi-agent pipeline set up like a small legal team: a triage analyst flags missing facts and asks for them; three researchers pull statutes, case law and regulator guidance in parallel; a sufficiency gate sends the team back until the research holds up; a currency check confirms the law is still good; a writer drafts in IRAC; five reviewers stress-test logic, clarity, citations, style and counter-arguments; a mediator consolidates; the writer revises up to three times; then a final polish. Sources come from two dedicated legal MCP servers: Legal Data Hunter (100+ jurisdictions, ingested from official registries like Légifrance and EUR-Lex) and CourtListener (US case law). Output: a formatted memo.docx with footnoted citations, a full source pack with every statute and case quoted verbatim and current-as-of dates, an honest verdict (approved or flagged for manual review), and a complete audit trail. It can learn your house style from your past memos. The trade: a full run takes 70–90 minutes and about 20–30% of a 5-hour window on the $200 Max plan. MIT-licensed and free. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_free-professional-cited-verifiable-memoranda-activity-7467470336482074624-zZGs)

## Sometimes I forget I live in a bubble (20 May 2026)

In my feed lawyers are forking MikeOSS, shipping projects in LegalQuants, writing skills and MCP servers; it feels like the whole profession has already moved. Then I step outside. A lawyer who actively uses AI told me about her team: out of 30, only 3–4 do anything meaningful with it; the rest paste a question into a generic chat once in a while. Four out of thirty, in 2026. Not building, just making AI a real part of the workflow. Fear of mistakes is the obvious explanation, but lawyers already rely on drafts from juniors, clauses from precedent banks and old templates, and review all of it anyway; AI output is not uniquely risky by default. So what is the real blocker: the billable hour punishing you for finishing in 3 hours instead of 12, no time to learn, or using AI still feeling like admitting you didn't do the work? Skills, incentives, trust, or culture? (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_sometimes-i-forget-i-live-in-a-bubble-in-activity-7462750467803115520-Y0MP)

## Subagents vs Agent Teams in Claude (13 May 2026)

Chat runs prompt-by-prompt — you steer every step. An agent has a goal, a process, and an exit condition; it runs on its own and stops when the goal is met. Two ways to spawn agents in Claude, both included in the subscription. Subagents (Cowork and Claude Code): give each subagent a role, an orchestrator runs them in parallel (or in a pipeline you define), each works in its own context and reports findings. For a service agreement I might run four — risk, compliance, commercial, IP — and the orchestrator pulls the findings together. Subagents don't see each other; you get the synthesis. Hint from Oleg Blinov: add a writer to the team. The writer edits, the reviewers (same subagents, fresh instances) score 1–100 on their angles, the writer revises until every reviewer gives at least 90. Each round uses fresh reviewers so they don't see previous scores. Agent Teams (Claude Code, still experimental): same idea, but agents are independent, see each other, and message directly — no scoring rounds, continuous back-and-forth. You watch it live and can jump in to correct anyone. Costs more tokens, more setup; Pro probably can't keep up. What you get back: a draft already shaped by the pushback you'd otherwise add yourself. Subagents for tasks you'd split among separate people; Agent Teams for the ones you'd put in a room together to argue and find the truth. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_build-your-ai-team-in-claude-activity-7460240042469330944-GkXp)

## Free knowledge base your team's Claude can read (4 May 2026)

What does the EDPB say about automated decision-making in credit scoring after Schufa? Anyone who's tried to answer that knows the problem — PDFs scattered across folders nobody opens, named exactly the way the regulator named them. Twenty minutes to find the right doc; next month, same twenty minutes. Stack: a Google Drive folder shared with the team, mirrored locally as an Obsidian vault. Obsidian is free and opens any folder of markdown files. Marker and Docxer plugins convert PDF and DOCX to clean markdown on right-click. Claude Desktop with the Drive MCP reads the whole base on request. Add a colleague to Drive and they have the same base — no onboarding. How the AI side works: Claude scans the index, picks the doc it needs, and reads only what's relevant. Drop a new file in? "Claude, refresh the index." Thirty seconds and it's part of the base. The trick that makes this work is the indexes — one per folder, one entry per document with a short summary. Same logic as a library catalog. One caveat: this is fine for public reference material — guidelines, published court rulings, regulators' standard forms. For confidential materials, anonymize first or keep them outside the AI's reach. Local LLMs are an option on that side. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_how-to-build-free-kb-for-your-team-activity-7456985032306388993-i7OA)

## PII Shield v2 — anonymize the matter, not the document (28 Apr 2026)

10 contracts on your desk. Same counterparties across half of them. You want Claude to analyze them as one matter, without a single client name reaching the Claude API. That's what PII Shield v2 does. v1 worked one file at a time — "Acme Corp" became ORG_1 in one document and could be ORG_3 in another; cross-document analysis broke. v2 holds the matter, not the document: "Acme Corp" stays the same placeholder across all 10 files. Each anonymized file carries the session ID, so open one in 4 weeks, deanonymize, and the real data comes back. Export the matter as an encrypted archive (AES-GCM via scrypt), a colleague imports with the passphrase and continues on their laptop. PII never moves between you and never reaches the API. Entity-review panel now lives inside Claude Desktop, not a separate browser — mark a missed entity once, it propagates across the session; reject a false positive once, it's gone everywhere. Tested on 50 English-language documents: 95% recall, low false positives. One-drop install, no Python. Next: a CLI so PII Shield runs on a folder of contracts from any tool, not just Claude. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_pii-shield-v2-ugcPost-7454803663107096576-oGbO)

## Stop shipping memos as 14-page .docx (21 Apr 2026)

Honest question to legal colleagues: aren't you tired of writing boring memos? Tech founders open a 14-page .docx in Times New Roman, see numbered paragraphs and a nine-line "Executive Summary," and ask privately: could you just tell me what this means? With Claude's design tool I turned the Duke Memo into a web page in a single prompt — headings that breathe, sections you can navigate, citations that look like citations. Sometimes you ship both: the web version for the client to actually read, the document version for the file. Clients who enjoy reading your work tend to come back for more. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_honest-question-for-my-legal-colleagues-share-7452308266916884480-pMAQ)

## PII Shield + Human-in-the-Loop review (Apr 2026)

Two days after I shipped PII Shield (500+ reactions, 80+ comments) I spent a night building what people asked for. HITL review: a local web UI showing every detected entity color-coded in context — click to remove false positives, select text to add missed ones; all matching occurrences update automatically; Claude re-anonymizes with corrections, override data never touches the API. Plus an audit log of every MCP call (proof for compliance teams that only file paths and session IDs flow through the API) and an NER log of every detection decision, both on-disk under ~/.pii_shield/audit/. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_two-days-ago-i-shared-pii-shield-local-ugcPost-7445484144651984897-PCSE)

## Claude Cowork that never sees your client data (Apr 2026)

PII Shield is a Cowork Skill paired with a local MCP server. Connect a folder, type "write a risk memo for vendor_agreement.docx" — anonymization happens locally before Claude sees a thing. "John Smith" becomes <PERSON_1>, "Acme Corp" becomes <ORG_1>. Claude analyzes the anonymized version; PII Shield restores everything in the final .docx with the formatting you prefer. Detection runs on a GLiNER NER model plus custom recognizers; 90%+ of PII gets replaced automatically. Important nuance: connect documents as a folder, don't drag-attach to the message — attached files get rendered before tools run.

## An AI agent that follows citation chains (Mar 2026)

An AI agent opened a case-law database, ran a search, screened 24 results, picked the four that mattered, followed their citation chains (ILVA A/S → Deutsche Wohnen → Nacionalinis → TR v Land Hessen), and delivered a structured digest. I made coffee. Not keyword matching — actual research behavior. Claude read all four CJEU rulings (60-100 paragraphs each) plus the AG opinions, came back with a table mapping how the proportionality doctrine developed across all four. Claude Max ($100/mo) holds the thread across long legal texts; Pro loses context after ~40 paragraphs. Output isn't perfect — fifteen minutes of editing versus half a day reading and taking notes. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_an-ai-agent-opened-a-case-law-database-ran-activity-7441766600648810496-E6py)

## One memo and a Claude subscription (Mar 2026)

I took our strongest memo and fed it to Claude's Skill creation. It parsed the .docx XML, figured out fonts, spacing, heading hierarchy, quote indentation, risk-assessment layout — turned it into a reusable SKILL.md. Now I throw raw notes from a call at it and get back a properly-formatted memo: numbered sections, citations in original language, risk assessments per issue, actual .docx not markdown. Reproduces Roboto 12pt, 11pt italic quotes with left indent, justified, single spacing. Also matches my writing style and terminology. Took 20 minutes to set up. Works for memos, contracts, claims, policies, board resolutions. I still do the legal analysis. I just stopped doing the formatting. (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_one-memo-and-a-claude-subscription-thats-activity-7440289317366784000-yyQQ)

## Brand monitor — weekly trademark hunt (Mar 2026)

I deployed an AI agent that finds trademark infringers and pirated app builds every week. Two tracks: App Store — queries iTunes Search across countries, fuzzy-matches names and bundle IDs against registered trademarks, narrows ~1,000 listings to ~50 candidates, runs icon vision on the high-risk ones. Piracy — searches mod/cracked APK sites, parses download pages, collects evidence packages (screenshots, HTML, WHOIS) for confirmed violations. LLM layer scores risk, recommends action, ships a prioritized Excel report. Hours of manual work → ~20 minutes reviewing. Single SKILL.md file — drop into Claude or OpenClaw with your trademark and target countries. Repo: https://github.com/gregmos/Brand-monitor (Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/grigorii-moskalev_i-deployed-an-openclaw-ai-agent-to-find-trademark-activity-7439559446172835840-oP8n)

# PII Shield — full product page

## What it is

PII Shield is an open-source MCP server for Claude Desktop. The user drops a file into a connected folder; PII Shield reads it locally, replaces every name, ID, and number with placeholders, and only the anonymized text crosses the wire. After the model finishes, the real values are stitched back into the output on the user's machine. The original text never leaves the disk.

## Pipeline (how it flows)

The document is anonymized locally; only placeholder text reaches Claude. When the model is done, PII is stitched back in — without ever leaving your disk.

Stages:
1. **Document** (PDF · DOCX · TXT) — has PII
2. **PII Shield** — anonymize (LOCAL)
3. **Claude API** — analyze placeholders (REMOTE)
4. **PII Shield** — restore (LOCAL)
5. **Result** — analysis with real names

PII never leaves the machine. Anonymization and restoration both happen locally.

### MCP call sequence (developer view)

- Document → Shield: `anonymize_file({ file_path, session_id? })` → `{ session_id, entity_count, output_path, … }`
- Shield → Claude API: Claude reads `output_path` from the connected folder. Only placeholders cross the wire.
- Claude API → Shield: model output flows back as text — still placeholder-only.
- Shield → Result: `deanonymize_docx({ file_path, session_id })` or `deanonymize_text({ text, session_id })` stitches the real PII back in, locally.

### Transform example (before/after Claude sees)

Before (real document):
- John Smith signed the NDA.
- ACME Corp v. Globex.
- Contact: john@acme.example
- Amount: €120,000 via IBAN CY17…
- UK NIN: AB123456C · DOB 1984-06-12

After (what Claude sees over API):
- `<PERSON_1>` signed the NDA.
- `<ORG_1>` v. `<ORG_2>`.
- Contact: `<EMAIL_1>`
- Amount: `<MONEY_1>` via IBAN `<IBAN_1>`
- UK NIN: `<UK_NIN_1>` · DOB `<DATE_1>`

## Why this exists

Pasting client material into a consumer LLM is both a privacy and a privilege problem.

A federal court has already confirmed the privilege side directly: in *United States v. Heppner* (S.D.N.Y., February 2026), documents a defendant created with consumer Claude were ruled outside attorney-client privilege. An AI tool is not an attorney and owes no duty of confidentiality.

PII Shield runs the redaction step before the model sees anything. It's an MCP server for Claude Desktop — drop a file, Claude receives placeholders like `<PERSON_1>` and `<ORG_2>`, and the real values are stitched back into the output on your machine. The original text never leaves your disk.

### v1 → v2 · the rewrite (developer view)

v1 was Python + Presidio + spaCy — every install fought Claude Desktop's bundled runtime. v2 is a complete Node.js rewrite over `onnxruntime-node` + `@xenova/transformers`: same detection coverage, no Python.

Plugin: 700 KB on Windows/Linux (host Node), or 83 MB on macOS (bundled Node 24.15.0). The 634 MB `gliner-pii-base-v1.0` model installs on-demand via an in-chat panel — never bundled in the artefact. CI runs the matrix on Ubuntu/Windows/macOS × Node 18/20.

Current builds are always on https://github.com/gregmos/PII-Shield/releases/latest; the v1 Python build remains downloadable from older tags for legacy installs.

## Skill modes (six task-shaped workflows)

The companion `pii-contract-analyze` skill ships six task-shaped modes. Each runs the same anonymize → analyze → deanonymize pipeline, just optimized for a different deliverable:

1. **MEMO** — legal memorandum on a contract or set of contracts
2. **REDLINE** — tracked-changes redline against a baseline document
3. **SUMMARY** — short-form summary
4. **COMPARISON** — diff two documents
5. **BULK** — process up to five files in one session
6. **ANONYMIZE** — anonymize without analysis (handoff use)

## What it detects

17 country-specific patterns on top of generic name and entity detection.

### Jurisdictions (17 EU + UK patterns)

- **United Kingdom** (5): NIN · NHS · Passport · CRN · Driving licence
- **Germany** (2): Tax ID · Social security
- **France** (2): NIR · CNI
- **Italy** (2): Fiscal code · VAT
- **Spain** (2): DNI · NIE
- **Cyprus** (2): TIC · National ID
- **EU-wide** (2): VAT · Passport

### Generic, jurisdiction-agnostic

person · org · location · email · phone · IBAN · credit card · crypto wallet · US SSN · US EIN · medical licence · money · date

### Detection method (developer view)

- **NER (zero-shot)** via GLiNER: person, org, location
- **Regex / pattern**: all 17 jurisdiction patterns + email · phone · IBAN · credit card · crypto · SSN · EIN · licences · money · date

## Quick start

Four steps. No terminal.

1. **Download the artefacts** — pick the `.mcpb` for your OS plus the contract-analyze skill. All three are attached to the latest release: https://github.com/gregmos/PII-Shield/releases/latest
2. **Install in Claude Desktop** — Settings → Extensions → Advanced Settings → Install extension. On first call, PII Shield runs `npm ci --ignore-scripts` to install pinned runtime deps (`onnxruntime-node`, `@xenova/transformers`, `gliner`) into `~/.pii_shield/deps/` — 2-3 minutes once per machine, instant thereafter.
3. **Connect a folder** with your documents — Claude Desktop → Settings → Connected folders. (Don't drag-attach files into the chat — the raw document hits the API before PII Shield can intercept.)
4. **Use it from a chat** — pick the `pii-contract-analyze` skill, tell Claude what you need.

### First-run model install

The first time you ask Claude to anonymize, PII Shield notices the GLiNER model isn't on disk and opens an in-chat install panel: download (~634 MB, fetched by browser) and install ZIP (validated, atomic-extracted into `~/.pii_shield/models/`). Subsequent runs skip the panel.

### Build & verify locally (developer)

```
npm ci --ignore-scripts --legacy-peer-deps
npm run build              # esbuild bundle
npm run smoke              # node scripts/smoke-protocol.mjs
npm test                   # 8 suites, incl. multi-doc HITL & session archival
```

CI runs the same matrix on Ubuntu / Windows / macOS × Node 18 / 20.

## Compliance & audit

Three logs, all on-disk:

- `~/.pii_shield/audit/mcp_audit.log` — every MCP call (anonymize, deanonymize, export, import) with timestamp, file path, entity counts.
- `~/.pii_shield/audit/ner_init.log` — model initialization events.
- `~/.pii_shield/audit/pii_shield_server.log` — server lifecycle.

No telemetry, no remote logging endpoint. If your DPO asks "what did the tool do with that file at 14:02 UTC," the answer is on your filesystem.

### Storage layout (developer)

Encrypted handoff: `export_session(passphrase)` → `.pii-session` archive (AES-GCM + scrypt-derived key). Mappings live at `~/.pii_shield/mappings/`, models at `~/.pii_shield/models/`, audit trail appendable at `~/.pii_shield/audit/mcp_audit.log`. Session TTL 7 days, configurable. All inputs validated with Zod (TypeScript strict). Off-network by design — no telemetry endpoint to disable.

## Features

- **Zero PII in API** — every call to Claude carries placeholders only.
- **GLiNER NER** — `gliner-pii-base-v1.0` running on `onnxruntime-node`, on-device.
- **HITL review** — `start_review` opens an in-chat iframe to add/remove/edit detected entities; `apply_review_overrides` propagates corrections across all occurrences in the session.
- **Entity dedup** — identical entities collapse to one placeholder; reduces output token noise.
- **Cross-session deanon** — `deanonymize_docx` works in any chat using the docx's embedded session_id.
- **Multi-file sessions** — pass `session_id` to `anonymize_file` to extend a session; identical entities across files share placeholders.
- **Encrypted handoff** — `export_session(passphrase)` → `.pii-session` archive (AES-GCM via scrypt). Hand off to a colleague with just the passphrase.
- **On-device audit logging** — every action recorded to `~/.pii_shield/audit/mcp_audit.log`.

## MCP tools (developer view — 17 tools, 4 groups)

### Anonymize (4)
- `anonymize_file` — preferred entry point. Anonymizes PDF/DOCX/TXT. PII stays on host.
- `anonymize_text` — anonymize raw string.
- `anonymize_docx` — DOCX-specific, preserves formatting.
- `anonymize_next_chunk` — chunked processing for documents >5000 chars.

### Review (5)
- `start_review` — open the HITL iframe inside Claude Desktop.
- `apply_review_overrides` — apply user edits, propagate across the session.
- `get_full_anonymized_text` — return full anonymized text for piping.
- `deanonymize_text` — restore PII placeholders → real values in a string.
- `deanonymize_docx` — restore PII in DOCX using its embedded `session_id`.

### Session (3)
- `export_session` — pack mapping + anonymized files into encrypted `.pii-session` archive.
- `import_session` — unlock and load a `.pii-session` archive.
- `get_mapping` — inspect the placeholder ↔ value mapping.

### Utility (5)
- `scan_text` — preview-only entity detection without creating a session.
- `list_entities` — list all detected entities, grouped by type.
- `find_file` — resolve a path inside a connected folder.
- `resolve_path` — relative or absolute path resolution.
- `install_model_from_download` — install GLiNER from a local download.

### Round-trip example

```
// 1. anonymize a file — original stays on disk; only placeholders cross the wire
→ anonymize_file({ file_path: "~/contracts/nda.docx" })
← { status: "success",
    session_id: "m9q8x4-7b5a91",
    entity_count: 14,
    output_path: ".../nda.anon.txt",
    docx_output_path: ".../nda.anon.docx",
    by_type: { PERSON: 4, ORG: 3, MONEY: 2, ... } }

// 2. Claude reads output_path and drafts a memo using placeholders only

// 3. restore PII into the draft, locally
→ deanonymize_text({ text: draft, session_id: "m9q8x4-7b5a91" })
← { status: "success",
    deanonymized_text: "...John Smith signed the NDA..." }
```

All inputs validated with Zod. Errors return MCP-protocol-shaped `{ isError: true, content: [...] }` instead of throwing.

## Stack

Built with: Node.js 18+, MCP (Model Context Protocol), GLiNER, onnxruntime-node, @xenova/transformers, DOCX (pure JS), pdf-parse, AES-GCM / scrypt, MIT license.

Tested on: Ubuntu / Windows / macOS, Node 18 / 20, 8 test suites, MCP protocol smoke test, Zod schema validation.
